title: Blood in Stool: Guaiac vs Immunochemical Tests and the Apt Test
summary: Learn why the guaiac test reacts with any heme while FIT reads human globin that is digested before the colon, which interferences fool each test, why a positive guaiac test is not a cancer diagnosis, and how the Apt test separates fetal from maternal blood.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 23 Trap 2 (iFOB insensitive to upper GI bleeding; guaiac detects heme), Trap 3 (positive guaiac is not colorectal cancer; dietary and drug interference; vitamin C false negatives) and Hit 15 (Apt test: pink = fetal, yellow-brown = maternal). Checked against Young 2015, Méndez 2025, Salisbury 2021, Piccirillo 2024 and Kocic 2023 (all read as Europe PMC full text). Qualified: the sources add that stool blood tests are not validated for working up acute upper GI bleeding (register flag rv-ifob-ugib-context), and the reviewer’s fixed “5–10% of positives are cancer” and “hold ≥72 h” are given as kit- and setting-dependent (PPV for cancer 2.5–10.7% across kits; restrictions 2 to 7 days) (register flag rv-gfobt-ppv-restriction). Not taught: the Number Vault iFOB detection figure (50 μg Hb/g) and guaiac 5–10 mL/day threshold and 30–50% sensitivity; turnips as an interferent (not found in the sources read).

objectives: State which part of hemoglobin the guaiac test and the fecal immunochemical test (FIT) detect, and why FIT is selective for colorectal bleeding.
List common causes of false-positive and false-negative guaiac results and explain why a positive result is not a cancer diagnosis.
Perform and interpret the Apt alkali denaturation test to separate fetal from maternal blood.

scenes.title: Whose blood, and from where?
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: three requests. (1) An adult with black, tarry stools; an immunochemical stool test (FIT) is ordered “to confirm an upper GI bleed” and comes back negative. (2) An outpatient guaiac card is positive two days after steak and raw broccoli. (3) A two-day-old breastfed newborn vomits blood; the mother has cracked nipples. Question token: “Whose blood, and from where?”

cues.text: Invented case one: an adult with black, tarry stools. An immunochemical stool test is ordered to confirm an upper bleed, and it comes back negative.
Case two: a guaiac card is positive, two days after a steak dinner and raw broccoli.
Case three: a two-day-old breastfed baby vomits blood, and the mother has cracked nipples. Whose blood is it, and where did it come from?

scenes.title: Heme or globin: what each test sees
scenes.altText: Schematic hemoglobin molecule split into its heme part and its globin (protein) part. Left card, guaiac fecal occult blood test (gFOBT): heme has peroxidase-like activity; when hydrogen peroxide developer is added, heme drives oxidation of guaiac on the card and it turns blue. Right card, fecal immunochemical test (FIT): antibodies against the globin of HUMAN hemoglobin; quantitative versions are often instrument-read, with an adjustable cut-off. Bottom token: globin is digested by proteolytic enzymes in the stomach and small intestine, so FIT is selective for colorectal bleeding.

cues.text: Hemoglobin has two parts: heme, and the globin protein. The two stool tests look at different parts.
The guaiac test uses heme. Add the hydrogen peroxide developer, heme drives oxidation of guaiac on the card, and it turns blue.
The immunochemical test, FIT, uses antibodies against the globin of human hemoglobin. Quantitative versions are often read by an instrument, with a cut-off that can be adjusted.
Globin is digested by protein-cutting enzymes in the stomach and small intestine. So FIT is selective for bleeding from the colon and rectum.

props.label: Globin digested in stomach + small bowel → FIT sees colorectal blood

scenes.title: Interference and the upper-GI blind spot
scenes.altText: Left card, guaiac false positives: animal heme (red meat), raw fruit and vegetables with peroxidase activity (for example broccoli, cauliflower, horseradish, melons), aspirin, NSAIDs and anticoagulants; false negatives: vitamin C, an antioxidant that blocks the colour reaction. Restrictions start days before collection (2 to 7 days in one review; follow the kit insert). Right card, FIT: no dietary or drug restrictions needed; not affected by dietary peroxidases. Bottom card: in one study up to 100 mL of swallowed blood was missed by some immunochemical methods but detected by guaiac. Token: neither test is validated for working up an acute upper GI bleed.

cues.text: Because guaiac reacts with any heme-like peroxidase activity, it is easily fooled. Red meat, and raw vegetables or fruit with peroxidase activity, such as broccoli or horseradish, can make it falsely positive. So can aspirin, other anti-inflammatory drugs and anticoagulants.
Vitamin C works the other way: an antioxidant that blocks the blue reaction, giving false negatives. Restrictions start days before collection; follow the kit insert.
FIT needs no diet or drug restrictions, and its antibodies ignore animal heme and plant peroxidases.
But FIT largely misses upper bleeding. In one study, up to one hundred millilitres of swallowed blood was missed by some immunochemical methods, yet picked up by guaiac.
And neither stool test is validated for diagnosing an acute upper bleed. Black, tarry stool calls for clinical assessment and endoscopy, not a stool card.

props.label: Melena → clinical assessment + endoscopy, not a stool card

scenes.title: The Apt test: baby blood or mother’s blood?
scenes.altText: Steps of the Apt (Apt-Downey) alkali denaturation test, drawn as a schematic row of tubes: (1) mix the bloody material with water to lyse red cells; (2) centrifuge; (3) mix the pink supernatant with 1% sodium hydroxide; (4) read the colour after about 2 minutes. Result cards: stays PINK = fetal hemoglobin, which resists alkali; turns YELLOW-BROWN = adult hemoglobin, which is less stable and converts to hematin. Hook answers card: (1) FIT is the wrong test for an upper bleed: globin is digested; (2) the guaiac positive may reflect diet; (3) Apt test to separate swallowed maternal blood from the baby’s own bleeding.

cues.text: Newborns can swallow their mother’s blood, during delivery or from cracked nipples. The Apt test, an alkali denaturation test, tells maternal blood from the baby’s own.
Mix the bloody material with water to burst the red cells, centrifuge, then add one percent sodium hydroxide to the supernatant and read it after about two minutes.
Fetal hemoglobin resists alkali, so the fluid stays pink. Adult hemoglobin is less stable: it converts to hematin and turns yellow-brown.

Back to the hook. Case one: FIT is the wrong tool for an upper bleed. Case two: the guaiac positive may reflect the steak and broccoli. Case three: run the Apt test; yellow-brown points to swallowed maternal blood.

props.label: Swallowed maternal blood? Delivery · cracked nipples

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “Order FIT to work up a suspected upper GI bleed” (✓ human globin is digested before the colon; FIT is selective for colorectal bleeding, and stool tests are not validated for acute upper bleeding); “A positive guaiac test means colorectal cancer” (✓ in screening studies only a minority of positives had cancer — positive predictive value roughly 2.5–11% depending on the kit; diet and drugs cause false positives; follow up with colonoscopy); “Apt test: pink means maternal blood” (✓ pink = fetal hemoglobin, which resists alkali; yellow-brown = adult).

cues.text: Trap one: order an immunochemical test for a suspected upper bleed. No: globin is digested before it reaches the colon, so FIT sees colorectal bleeding.

Trap two: a positive guaiac test means cancer. No: in screening studies, only a small minority of positives had cancer, and diet or drugs can cause false positives. A positive result leads to colonoscopy, not a diagnosis.
Trap three: in the Apt test, pink means the mother’s blood. No: pink is fetal hemoglobin, which resists alkali. Adult blood turns yellow-brown.

props.title: ✗ “Guaiac positive = cancer.”

scenes.title: Stain, name tag, tough baby blood
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Guaiac sees the STAIN (any heme, from any animal, from anywhere in the gut); FIT reads the human NAME TAG (globin), which is torn off in the stomach and small bowel; baby blood is TOUGH — it stays pink in lye.” Tokens: stain = guaiac · name tag = FIT · tough = fetal Hb. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: guaiac sees the stain, any heme, from any animal, from anywhere in the gut. FIT reads the human name tag, the globin, which is torn off in the stomach and small bowel. And baby blood is tough: it stays pink in lye.

Where it breaks: heme is also broken down by colonic bacteria, so guaiac misses some bleeding too; a FIT positive is not specific, because benign lesions bleed; and FIT cut-offs and kit performance vary.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Guaiac = any heme (diet, drugs, upper GI) · FIT = human globin, colorectal”, “Apt: pink = fetal Hb · yellow-brown = adult Hb”.

cues.text: Guaiac tests react with heme and other peroxidase activity, so diet, some drugs and upper bleeding can all turn them positive, immunochemical tests read human globin, which is mostly digested when bleeding starts above the colon, and in the Apt test fetal hemoglobin stays pink in alkali while adult hemoglobin turns yellow-brown.

props.label: Guaiac = any heme · FIT = human globin, colorectal
Apt: pink = fetal Hb · yellow-brown = adult Hb

explanation.what: Plain language: the guaiac card changes colour with anything that behaves like the iron part of blood, from any animal and any part of the gut. The immunochemical test looks for the protein part of human blood, which gets digested if the bleeding is high up. The Apt test uses lye to tell a baby’s blood from its mother’s. Scientific terms: guaiac fecal occult blood test (gFOBT), pseudoperoxidase activity of heme, hydrogen peroxide developer, fecal immunochemical test (FIT), human globin, proteolysis, positive predictive value (PPV), Apt (Apt-Downey) alkali denaturation test, fetal hemoglobin (HbF), hematin.
explanation.why: Heme survives passage from the upper gut well enough to turn a guaiac card blue, while globin is digested by gastric and small-bowel proteases, so FIT mainly reflects colorectal blood. Because guaiac chemistry is a simple oxidation, dietary heme, plant peroxidases and antioxidants interfere. Fetal hemoglobin is more resistant to alkali denaturation than adult hemoglobin.
explanation.measure: gFOBT: stool on guaiac paper, add hydrogen peroxide developer, blue = positive; dietary and drug restrictions before collection (2 to 7 days in one review; follow the kit). FIT: antibody to human globin, often quantitative with an adjustable cut-off, no restrictions. Apt: lyse in water, centrifuge, add 1% NaOH to supernatant, read after about 2 min: pink = fetal, yellow-brown = adult.
explanation.differs: gFOBT (heme; detects upper and lower GI blood; diet- and drug-sensitive) vs FIT (human globin; selective for colorectal bleeding; no restrictions). Apt: fetal (stays pink) vs maternal/adult (yellow-brown).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: pick the test that misses upper GI bleeding, name a food or vitamin that interferes with guaiac, reject “positive guaiac = cancer”, or read an Apt test colour.

questions.stem: A patient with a bleeding duodenal ulcer has black, tarry stools, but a fecal immunochemical test (FIT) is negative. What best explains the negative result?

options.text: Globin from upper GI blood is digested by proteolytic enzymes before it reaches the colon
options.rationale: Correct. FIT antibodies target human globin, which is degraded in the stomach and small intestine, so FIT is selective for colorectal bleeding.

options.text: Vitamin C in the diet blocked the colour reaction
options.rationale: Incorrect. Vitamin C causes false negatives in the guaiac test, whose chemistry is an oxidation; FIT is an immunoassay.

options.text: FIT cross-reacts with animal heme, which masks human blood
options.rationale: Incorrect. FIT antibodies are specific for human globin and are not affected by dietary heme.

options.text: The hydrogen peroxide developer was omitted
options.rationale: Incorrect. A peroxide developer is part of the guaiac test, not FIT.

questions.stem: Which factor can make a guaiac fecal occult blood test falsely POSITIVE but does not affect a fecal immunochemical test?

options.text: Eating rare red meat the day before collection
options.rationale: Correct. Animal heme (myoglobin and hemoglobin) has peroxidase-like activity that turns guaiac blue; FIT detects only human globin.
Incorrect. Vitamin C is an antioxidant that causes false-NEGATIVE guaiac results.
Incorrect. This is true colorectal bleeding, which both tests are designed to detect.
Incorrect. This is real blood, not interference; guaiac may detect it because heme survives, whereas FIT usually misses it because globin is digested.

questions.stem: Blood-stained vomitus from a 2-day-old newborn is mixed with water and centrifuged; the supernatant is mixed with 1% sodium hydroxide and stays pink after 2 minutes. What does this indicate?

options.text: Fetal hemoglobin: the blood is the baby’s own, so a neonatal source must be sought
options.rationale: Correct. Fetal hemoglobin resists alkali denaturation and stays pink.
Incorrect. Adult (maternal) hemoglobin is less stable in alkali and turns yellow-brown.
Incorrect. The test distinguishes fetal from adult hemoglobin; a pink supernatant after alkali indicates alkali-resistant fetal hemoglobin.

options.text: The test is invalid because adult hemoglobin should stay pink
options.rationale: Incorrect. This reverses the principle: adult hemoglobin converts to hematin and turns yellow-brown.

claims.text: gFOBT detects heme via peroxidase-like oxidation of guaiac with peroxide developer; FIT detects human globin with antibodies, often quantitative.
Globin is digested in the stomach and small intestine, so FIT is selective for colorectal bleeding; gFOBT detects upper and lower GI blood; up to 100 mL ingested blood missed by some FITs.
gFOBT false positives from red meat, peroxidase-rich raw foods, aspirin/NSAIDs/anticoagulants; vitamin C false negatives; restrictions 2 to 7 days; FIT needs none.
claims.note: The reviewer’s fixed “≥72 h” is given as 2 to 7 days in Méndez 2025; the lesson says to follow the kit insert (register flag rv-gfobt-ppv-restriction).

claims.text: Only a minority of positive guaiac screens have cancer (PPV for cancer about 2.5–10.7% across kits and settings); positives prompt colonoscopy.
Stool occult blood tests are not validated for diagnosing acute upper GI bleeding.
Apt test: water lysis, centrifuge, 1% NaOH, read ~2 min; pink = fetal Hb, yellow-brown = adult Hb (hematin); used to exclude swallowed maternal blood in neonates.
Reviewer Number Vault figures: iFOB detection 50 μg Hb/g; guaiac positive at >5–10 mL blood/day with 30–50% sensitivity; turnips as an interferent.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 23 Trap 2 says guaiac “works for upper bleeds”. Young 2015 and Salisbury 2021 confirm gFOBT can detect upper GI blood while FIT largely cannot, but Salisbury 2021 and Méndez 2025 add that stool occult blood testing is not validated for diagnosing acute upper GI bleeding and is commonly misused for overt bleeding; the lesson teaches the analytical point with that context (register flag rv-ifob-ugib-context).

Ch. 23 Trap 3 gives “only 5–10% of guaiac positives are malignancy” and “hold interferents ≥72 h”. Young 2015 reports PPV for cancer of about 2.5–10.7% depending on kit and setting, and Méndez 2025 gives restrictions of 2 to 7 days; the lesson teaches these as kit- and setting-dependent (register flag rv-gfobt-ppv-restriction).
